extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, painters, critics, and general connoisseurs (18th‑century literary/art audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing 'easy' poetry (and related remarks on high/poetical painting): how diction, structure, and choice of ornament determine ease and dignity; also principles for grand painting (imitating nature, composition, contrast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy poetry definition
rubrics_metrics.description: "Easy poetry is that in which natural thoughts are expressed without violence to the language.", i.e. the discriminating character of ease consists principally in the diction; all true poetry requires that the sentiments be natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid any violence to language: harsh or daring figures, transposition, unusual acceptations of words, and any licence which would be avoided by a writer of prose. "Where any artifice appears in the construction of the verse, that verse is no longer easy." Examples cited: Pope's Iliad first lines are distorted by inversions, superfluities, and harsh metaphor; artifice produces obscurity and ruggedness even if pardoned in longer works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superfluous epithets and needless ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Any epithet which can be ejected without diminution of the sense, any curious iteration of the same word, and all unusual, though not ungrammatical structure of speech, destroy the grace of easy poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim lines of epithets added only to lengthen the line. Beware of inserting words merely for metrical or rhetorical show; such superfluities clog and rob the verse of ease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and fashionable barbarisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation, however opposite to ease, is sometimes mistaken for it; those who aspire to gentle elegance collect female phrases and fashionable barbarisms and imagine that style to be easy which custom has made familiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate colloquial or modish phraseology with natural ease; such expressions are transient and will date the poem. Example parody given (verses to a 'countess cutting paper') as an affectation anti‑pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelessness of easy poetry (avoid mode‑dependent language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Easy poetry's prerogative is to be understood as long as the language lasts; modes of speech that owe their prevalence to modish folly die away with their inventors and their meaning becomes unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor language and structures that endure rather than catchphrases or fleeting fashions—avoid style that will be unintelligible once a mode passes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease admits sublimity (simplicity compatible with greatness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ease, though it excludes pomp, will admit greatness; simplicity does not preclude sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can write lines that are both easy and sublime (examples: lines in Cato's soliloquy). Pursue natural diction even when expressing grand or lofty sentiments—great thoughts do not require ornate, convoluted diction to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease is hard to sustain over long passages
rubrics_metrics.description: To require from any author many pieces of easy poetry would be to oppress him with too hard a task; producing a few couplets graced only by naked elegance and simple purity requires much care and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is easier to write many lines swelled with epithets and figures than to sustain sustained ease; expect effort and careful selection to maintain natural diction across extended work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct sense of 'imitate nature' for painting (general, not mechanical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim 'imitate nature' must be understood: the painter of genius studies nature to direct the imagination toward invariable, great and general ideas, not to produce mere mechanical relief that seems real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If excellence consisted only in literal imitation, painting would be a mechanical art. Genius avoids minute drudgery; the grand style requires selecting universal forms that stir imagination rather than slavishly reproducing accidental detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand style vs minute exactness (Italian vs Dutch distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Italian attends only to the invariable, the great and general ideas inherent in universal nature; the Dutch attend to literal truth and minute exactness in detail. The naturalness admired in the Dutch is of a lower order relative to the grand style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to unite contrarieties (e.g., Dutch literalness with Italian grandeur); one kind of beauty will give place to another and mixing destroys the efficacy of each. For the grand style prefer idealized, generalized forms rather than petty peculiarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and contrast (pyramidal principle, flowing line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use contrast and compositional disposition to produce nobleness and dignity—e.g., arrange figures so middle ones are on higher ground, extremities stooping or lying, forming the group into a pyramid; use flowing lines to create grace and avoid static, equally posed figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast poses, heights, and gestures to avoid monotony and create a sense of movement and hierarchy. Pay attention to drapery disposition and the flowing line that constitutes grace and beauty; avoid symmetrical, identical stances across figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper degree of enthusiasm (balance imagination and restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be too great indulgence of imagination (producing incoherent monsters) as well as too great restraint (producing lifeless insipidity); intimate knowledge of the passions and good sense must determine limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a measured enthusiasm: Michael Angelo sometimes transgressed limits (sublime or ridiculous), but his works escaped contempt. Know when energy serves expression and when it becomes excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mechanical realism from genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical naturalness or mechanical fidelity (making an object look as if you could pick it up) is not equivalent to greatness; fine literal rendering does not alone justify comparison with masters like Raphael or Michael Angelo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connoisseurs should not equate skill in rendering petty objects with grand genius; assess whether the work aspires to and attains higher imaginative aims rather than mere optical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the 'most general' or archetypal form for beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can judge beauty of a species without seeing many individuals; the painter selects the most beautiful as the most general form of nature—the invariable, central form toward which nature inclines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study many specimens to distinguish accidental blemishes from the invariable form; represent the archetypal or typical form rather than a singular accidental example. This justifies idealization in art to capture what is most frequently intended by nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake novelty or rarity for beauty of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty may cause admiration, but because something is uncommon is no proof it is beautiful; beauty (in the confined sense of form) is not equivalent to novelty or rarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'beauty' confined to form, do not conflate it with qualities like rarity, usefulness, colour, or smell. Avoid relying on novelty as the primary aesthetic claim.
